did_you_know.text: Did you know? The verb vayakhel is related to the word kahal, meaning an assembled community. The Torah emphasizes that the Tabernacle was built by the whole people, not only by a few individuals.

Did you know? In the Bible, the word melakhah can mean planned or skilled work, such as the craftsmen’s work on the Tabernacle. It does not refer to every movement, but to a particular kind of activity.
Did you know? The contribution to the Tabernacle is presented as a voluntary gift, not as a tax imposed on everyone. Later, so much material was donated that there was more than enough.
Did you know? The phrase avnei milu’im refers to stones set into mounts or frames, not simply loose stones. They were used to decorate the High Priest’s garments.
Did you know? The parokhet was an important curtain dividing the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies. It created a clear boundary within the Tabernacle.
Did you know? Leḥem ha-panim is called “bread of the Presence” because it was placed before God. The bread was replaced regularly rather than remaining on the table permanently.
Did you know? The menorah had seven lamps, although it is often pictured with six branches beside a central shaft. Olive oil was used to keep its light burning.
Did you know? The tent pegs and cords helped stabilize the Tabernacle and its courtyard. They made it sturdy while still allowing it to be dismantled and moved.
Did you know? The phrases “whose heart moved him” and “whose spirit prompted him” describe inner motivation and readiness. Both emphasize that the giving came from personal choice.
Did you know? Spinning means turning fibers into thread before they can be woven into cloth. The Torah presents it as a skilled and important part of building the Tabernacle.
Did you know? In the Bible, “wisdom of heart” means more than emotion; it includes practical talent, understanding, and skill. In Bezalel’s case, this wisdom appeared in careful creative work.
Did you know? Bezalel did not work alone: God also gave him and Oholiab the ability to teach. In this way, the Tabernacle’s expertise was shared rather than kept by one person.
